We are thrilled to announce rig 0.11.0 (and 0.10.0), with lots of new
functionalities: user mode R installations, R package and project management
and much more. This is the second of three blog posts about the new rig
release. This post is about managing R packages.

The first post covered user mode R installations. The third will focus on
[project management](https://rig.r-lib.org/proj-guide.html).

[Full changelog on the rig web site](https://rig.r-lib.org/news.html).

## Introduction

The new `rig pkg` command lets you manage R packages: installing,
removing, and querying package dependencies. It supports CRAN-like
repositories, packages in git repositories (including on GitHub), URLs
pointing to package files and packages in local files and directories.

`rig pkg` is aimed at R users and developers who use a single (or a few)
package libraries. If you prefer to use project-specific libraries, you
probably want to use `rig proj` instead.

::: {.callout-note}
`rig pkg` is new and less battle-tested than other parts of rig.
Please report any issues you find on the [rig GitHub repository](
  https://github.com/r-lib/rig/issues).
:::

## Managing installed packages

`rig pkg list` lists installed packages in a library. `rig pkg remove`
removes a package from a library.
```text
❯ rig pkg list
559 packages (R 4.6.1, main: /Users/gaborcsardi/Library/R/arm64/4.6/library)

Package              Version      Built   Platform                   Source
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
abind                1.4-8        4.6.0   -                          RSPM
ade4                 1.7-24       4.6.0   aarch64-apple-darwin23     CRAN
adegenet             2.1.11       4.6.0   aarch64-apple-darwin23     CRAN
AdmixPoly            1.0.1        4.6.0   aarch64-apple-darwin20     RSPM
affy                 1.90.0       4.6.1   aarch64-apple-darwin23     RSPM
affyio               1.82.0       4.6.0   aarch64-apple-darwin20     RSPM
[...]
```

`rig pkg doctor` checks the health of your package library, identifying any
issues with installed packages or their dependencies: missing dependencies,
dependency conflicts, ABI conflicts, etc. It also tells you how to fix these
issues.
```text
❯ rig pkg doctor
3 problems (1 error, 2 warnings) in 559 packages (R 4.6.1, main: /Users/gaborcsardi/Library/R/arm64/4.6/library)

Package              Version   Severity   Problem   Details
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
00LOCK-dress.graph   -         warning    lock      lock directory left behind by an interrupted installation
dress.graph          -         warning    broken    no DESCRIPTION file
missoNet             1.5.1     error      missing   Imports ComplexHeatmap, not installed

To fix the errors, run:
  rig pkg install ComplexHeatmap

To remove the leftover lock directories, if no installation is running, run:
  rm -rf /Users/gaborcsardi/Library/R/arm64/4.6/library/00LOCK-dress.graph

To remove the broken packages, run:
  rm -rf /Users/gaborcsardi/Library/R/arm64/4.6/library/dress.graph

✗ Found 1 error in /Users/gaborcsardi/Library/R/arm64/4.6/library
```

## Installing packages

`rig pkg install` can install R packages from CRAN-like repositories,
git repositories, GitHub, URLs, and local paths. It uses the default R
version and the default package library (see below about libraries),
unless otherwise specified. It caches metadata and package files heavily,
avoids redundant downloads and installations, and performs downloads and
package builds in parallel. It uses the host OS's file cloning capabilities
to efficiently copy files when installing packages.

This is how installing a package into an empty library looks like, if the
package files are already cached:


### Version constraints

`rig pkg install` supports version constraints for packages. Request a
specific version of a package with `@==<version>`:
```text
❯ rig pkg install ggplot2@==4.0.2
```

If you are familiar with `~` and `^` version constraints from other languages,
you can use them with `rig pkg install` as well. E.g. to install the
latest version of the ggplot2 3.x.y series, you would run:
```text
❯ rig pkg install ggplot2@^3.0.0
```

### Dependency solver

The rig dependency solver makes sure that all package dependencies are
resolved correctly before installation. If the combination of packages
cannot be installed on the specified R version or platform, rig will report
an error and refuse to proceed with the installation. For example:

```text
❯ rig pkg install -r 4.0.5-x86_64 'testthat@>=3.3.0'
▶ Downloading binary package metadata
▶ Solving dependencies
✗ Cannot resolve dependencies for R 4.0.5 / x86_64-apple-darwin:
  Because testthat >=3.3.0 depends on R >=4.1.0 and you requested
  testthat >=3.3.0, the requested packages cannot be installed.
```

### Packages from git, GitHub, URLs, paths

If you are familiar with pak's syntax for installing packages from
various non-CRAN sources, you can use the same syntax with rig. E.g. a
GitHub package is simply `username/repo`. You can use the usual syntax
for tags, branches, pull requests:
```text
❯ rig pkg install r-lib/cli
❯ rig pkg install r-lib/cli@badcafe
❯ rig pkg install r-lib/cli@some-branch
❯ rig pkg install r-lib/cli#41
```

Prefix packages in git repositories with `git::`. To install a package
from a URL simply use the full URL. For a local path use a relative path
starting with `./`, `../` or `~/` or an absolute path:
```text
❯ rig pkg install .
❯ rig pkg install ./mypkg
❯ rig pkg install ../mypkg
❯ rig pkg install ~/works/mypkg
❯ rig pkg install /opt/src/mypkg
❯ rig pkg install ./mypkg_1.0.0.tar.gz
```

### Preferring binary packages

rig prefers to install the binary package for a certain package version if
it is available, instead of building and potentially compiling it from
source. By default it does not choose an older version over a newer one
just because a binary is available for the older version. The
`--prefer-binary` option changes this. Use it if you prefer older binary
packages over newer source packages:
```text
❯ rig pkg install --prefer-binary tidyverse
```

### Installing dependencies

To install the dependencies of a package, without installing the package
itself, use `--no-install-project`. This is especially useful to install
all dependencies of a package tree in the current working directory. The
second variant also installs soft (development) dependencies:
```text
❯ rig pkg install --no-install-project .
❯ rig pkg install --no-install-project --dev .
```

## Repositories

`rig pkg` subcommands always use the configured repositories, see the
`rig repos` command. They also have `--with-repos` and `--without-repos`
options to include or exclude specific repositories when performing a single
package operation, without modifying the configured repositories. E.g. to
query the version of a package on CRAN and P3M you can run:
```text
❯ rig pkg info otel --without-repos --with-repos=p3m --versions
otel — 2 versions (latest 0.2.0)

Version   Published    R          Deps
-------------------------------------------------------
0.1.0     2025-07-31   >= 3.6.0      0
0.2.0     2025-08-29   >= 3.6.0      0   ← latest
```

```text
❯ rig pkg info otel --without-repos --with-repos=cran --versions
otel — 1 version (latest 0.2.0)

Version   Published   R          Deps
-------------------------------------------------------
0.2.0     ?           >= 3.6.0      0   ← latest
```

`rig pkg deps` prints the dependencies of a package. `rig pkg tree` does
the same, but as a dependency tree. You can use these commands to query
non-CRAN-like packages. E.g. the dependency tree of the package in the


The `--dev` flag includes development dependencies as well.

## Package libraries

rig creates a user-level package library for each R installation by default.
(See the [rig FAQ](https://rig.r-lib.org/faq.html) why.) This is the package
library that `rig pkg` commands use by default.

The `rig library` command supports creating other package libraries, still
stored in the user's home directory. You can refer to them by name and make
them the default library for `rig pkg` commands with `rig library default`.

For example to create a temporary library and install the Shiny package from
GitHub into it, including development dependencies, you can run:

```sh
rig library add test
rig library default test
rig pkg install --dev rstudio/shiny
```

You can also use the `-l` or `--library` option of the `rig pkg` commands to
change the package library temporarily for one command, without changing the
default.

If you are using the macOS menu bar app, then you can also manage package
libraries through the app's interface.

## System requirements

On certain Linux systems rig supports automatic system requirements
installation. These are currently:

* Ubuntu Linux,
* RedHat Enterprise Linux and clones,
* openSUSE Linux and SUSE Linux Enterprise,
* Debian Linux,
* Fedora Linux,
* Alpine Linux.

For the automatic system requirements installation to work, rig must run
as the `root` user or with password-less `sudo` privileges to call the
system package manager.

### Not needed in user mode

Note that in user mode, rig installs the self-contained manylinux R build,
which does not require any system-level dependencies and also sets up
Posit's manylinux package repository, which has self-contained binaries for
most CRAN and Bioconductor packages. So in user mode you typically do not
need to worry about system-level dependencies.
